transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-06
Time: 09:30 PT
Duration: 45 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood CSM) -- Maya Patel (ClearHealth ML), Tom Rivers (ClearHealth SRE), Lena Ortiz (Product)

Summary: weekly POC sync to review benchmark results vs the baseline provider, discuss tuning steps (batching, kv cache, quantization), and align on next steps for on-prem network test. Some numbers vs baseline discussed; transcription has slight recognition errors on product names.

Topics: benchmark results, latency vs cost tradeoffs, quantization impact, dedicated vs hosted routing, network egress for on-prem test, next steps and owners.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava: hey everyone thanks for joining, we have 45 minutes on the agenda today, basically benchmark results review vs your current provider, quick tuning notes, and next steps. how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Maya: good thanks, excited to go through the numbers, we've been looking at the 95th p99 numbers, so yeah thanks for doing the runs.
[00:20] Diego: cool, i'll start with the baseline summary, we ran three families: hosted small-context (2k), medium 4k, and long 8k sequences. compared to the baseline provider (we'll call them baseline provider or baseco), our median latency was about 12% lower on 2k, 8% lower on 4k, and for 8k we see parity or slightly higher depending on quantization. throughput at peak was about 1.4x vs baseline on the dedicated config with batching enabled.
[00:45] Tom: wait can you repeat the 8k numbers, you said parity or higher, what's the p95 impact?
[00:52] Diego: sure, for 8k seq with float16 model we saw p95 at ~1.1s per token vs baseline 0.95s in one of their runs. so at 8k the baseline had a slightly lower per-token latency in that config, but our token cost was lower once you applied our kv cache and prefix caching on repeated prompts. the raw throughput (tokens/sec) was about the same.
[01:20] Ava: just to add, those baseline runs were using their newest kernel stack and gaussian compiler, we had to tune kernel selection for similar performance. we also noted their effective batch sizes were higher which helps throughput but pushes p95 up if you need single-request latency.
[01:35] Lena: so is that because they prioritize batching over SLO? our app needs a 95th latency under 2s for the user flow.
[01:43] Diego: for the 8k scenario the p95 we observed with our recommended toggle (continuous batching with latency cap at 200ms) was around 1.8s for end-to-end generation on typical prompts, so you're within your 2s SLO if you enable that policy. if you need stricter SLOs we can flip to reserved latency mode which reduces batching but increases cost a bit.
[02:08] Maya: can you explain the reserved latency mode and cost delta? numbers please.
[02:12] Ava: yes, reserved latency mode enforces smaller micro-batches and prioritizes latency, it increased token cost approx 18% in our runs compared to cost-optimized batching. with dedicated capacity and the cache hits we saw cost back down to about 6% over baseline in worst-case, and often lower for repetitive prompt patterns.
[02:33] Tom: i want to flag network egress — when you tested on our dev cluster the net egress added ~80ms per request in the earlier run, did you account for that in these numbers?
[02:42] Diego: great point, the numbers i quoted were measured on our test harness where network was colocated (no egress). the run we did via your dev cluster had the extra 70-90ms, which pushes the p95 for short requests notably. next week we proposed to run a dedicated on-prem network test to capture realistic numbers with your firewalls and proxy in path.
[03:02] Maya: ok please add that as action item.
[03:05] Ava: noted — diego you'll run the on-prem network run with tom next week.
[03:10] Diego: yes i'll coordinate with Tom and we'll do a few runs: float16, 4-bit quant and a 3-parameter kv cache hit pattern to show delta.
[03:20] Priya: quick question on quantization quality, our QA sees more hallucinations with aggressive 4-bit in some prompt categories, did you notice that?
[03:28] Diego: we did a short eval on the dev set, quality drop varied by prompt type. general completion tasks were fine, but retrieval-augmented prompts with many entities saw more token-level mistakes. we recommend running the model mix: use 4-bit for high-throughput logged endpoints and float16 or 8-bit for critical QA flows. we can set routing policy to send critical requests to a higher-quality variant.
[03:53] Maya: that's helpful. can you also share the eval prompts and the diff of outputs?
[03:58] Diego: yes we'll add the eval diffs to the benchmark spreadsheet.
[04:02] Ava: regarding autoscaling and burst capacity — you asked about peak season — our dedicated pools can burst to additional nodes, we saw near-linear throughput gains with scaled pools in the test harness. the cost model for burst is pay-as-you-go with minimum committed reserved capacity still covering baseline.
[04:20] Lena: what's the failure mode if burst capacity isn't available? we need graceful degradation.
[04:26] Diego: we have routing fallbacks: 1) route to a smaller model variant with similar semantics 2) route to hosted fallback region 3) queue with priority tokens. fallback adds latency but maintains correctness. we can prioritize critical traffic via route tags.
[04:44] Tom: security questions — for on-prem tests we need SSO and audit logs enabled. last time you sent docs, are the logs customizable retention windows?
[04:52] Ava: yes SAML SSO is supported, and audit log retention is configurable per plan; we can provide SOC 2 artifacts and an IL-2 style compliance primer. i'll re-share the security pack after this call.
[05:03] Maya: in the benchmark sheet i noticed a line 'kv cash' spelled wrong, probably transcription or a csv typo, but can you confirm how KV cache hit rate is measured?
[05:12] Diego: yes thats a typo in the spreadsheet, we measure KV cache hit rate by key equality on prefix hashes over a 24-hour workload sample; we report both exact hit rate and effective token savings. for your traffic the estimated token savings were 12% to 28% depending on prompt repetition.
[05:31] Lena: on routing and pricing, if we pin a model version for the pilot and roll to prod later, does the pricing change?
[05:38] Ava: you can pin model versions; pricing for dedicated capacity is primarily by reserved pool size and runtime (GPU type). pinning per se doesn't change unit token price unless you choose a premium tier model variant. we'll include example pricing scenarios in the sheet.
[05:52] Maya: any notes on kernel/compilers? you mentioned earlier you had to tune kernel selection vs the baseline.
[05:57] Diego: yes small detail — the baseline used a newer compiler stack that gives them a small edge on some attention patterns; we matched by selecting a different kernel set and enabling ffn-fusion on the runtime which improved latency by 6-9% on mixed prompts. these are runtime knobs we can flip in Private and Dedicated.
[06:18] Tom: durability — logs and metrics retention for our security team needs 12 months. can we get a compliance table?
[06:24] Ava: absolutely, I'll send the compliance table and the SOC2 section in the security pack.
[06:28] Priya: wrapping to next steps: Diego will run the 8k quant run and the on-prem network test with Tom, Ava will send pricing and security docs, Maya to provide prompt distribution and SLO. anything else?
[06:41] Maya: can you also include cost-per-1000 token comparisons vs baseline across the three seq lengths?
[06:46] Diego: yes that will be in the updated spreadsheet with raw logs attached.
[06:50] Ava: perfect. do we want another sync next week same time?
[06:54] Maya: yes same time works.
[06:56] Ava: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up in CRM and share the updated artifacts.
[07:00] End of recording
